papers.title: Long-term exposure to six gaseous air pollutants and risk of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: This Finnish population-nested case-control (FINPARK) study investigates the association between long-term exposure to six gaseous air pollutants and PD risk. Incident PD cases (n = 22,189) between 1996 and 2015 were identified from the Finnish medical reimbursement register maintained by the Finnish Social Security Institution. Age-, sex- and region-matched cases (n = 148,009) were identified from the Finnish population register. Time-weighted average air pollution exposure was modelled at the residential address for 16 years preceding the PD diagnosis. We observed a marginally increased risk for PD after higher levels of exposure to O3

papers.title: Kidney-inflammation-erythrocyte framework for Parkinson disease risk prediction and progression assessment.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder involving metabolic and peripheral pathological dysregulation. This study proposed a clinically accessible "Kidney-Inflammation-Erythrocyte" framework to characterize peripheral alterations in PD. We constructed and validated a nomogram for PD screening, identified factors associated with Hoehn and Yahr (H-Y) stages, and explored potential biological associations with disease progression using mediation analysis. 572 participants were included to examine the renal function markers, inflammatory indicators, and erythrocyte parameters. Firstly, after LASSO and multivariable logistic regression analysis, seven predictors, including age, sex, urea nitrogen, albumin, interleukin-6 (IL-6), C-reactive protein, and cystatin C, were used to build the nomogram, which showed good discrimination in the training and validation cohorts. Secondly, IL-6, cystatin C, and red blood cell count also showed stage-dependent changes across H-Y stages. Thirdly, after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, medication history, and comorbidities, mediation analysis showed significant total effects on H-Y stages, but no significant mediation pathways. In summary, this study demonstrates significant associations between the "Kidney-Inflammation-Erythrocyte" framework and PD, supporting the potential value of integrating routine laboratory markers for PD screening and disease monitoring. However, further mechanistic studies are needed to clarify how these peripheral alterations are associated with disease status and progression.

papers.title: Observation of α-Synuclein Droplets and Analysis of Aggregates Formed by Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation In Vitro.
papers.abstract: Aggregation of α-synuclein (αSyn) is a key event in the development of α-synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Recent studies have shown that αSyn undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and subsequently forms aggregates through a sol-gel phase transition. In this chapter, we describe methods for observing αSyn LLPS and analyzing the resulting aggregates in vitro.

papers.title: α-Synuclein Seeding Assay Using Dopaminergic Neurons from Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells.
papers.abstract: The α-synuclein (α-Syn) seeding assay using dopaminergic neurons (DNs) derived from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is a physiologically relevant cellular model for synucleinopathies. In this assay, exogenous α-Syn fibrils (seeds) are introduced into neurons to induce intracellular aggregation of endogenous α-Syn. The resulting aggregates are typically evaluated using immunostaining for phosphorylated α-Syn at serine 129 (pS129 α-Syn). Herein, a practical and reproducible protocol for performing α-Syn seeding assays in iPSC-derived DNs, including fibril preparation, transduction, and downstream evaluation using immunocytochemistry and Western blot analysis, is described.

papers.title: α-synuclein regulation of monoamine transporters: Implications for psychostimulant pharmacology and Parkinson disease.
papers.journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics

papers.title: Incretin-Based Therapies and the Gut-Brain Axis in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), originally developed for metabolic disorders, remain under active investigation as potential therapeutic candidates for neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, with clinical trials to date reporting both positive and negative findings. This scoping review critically synthesizes evidence from preclinical and clinical studies (n = 99), with a focus on the molecular pharmacodynamics of semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide, and lixisenatide, together with tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist (GLP-1/GIP RA) discussed separately given its distinct receptor pharmacology. In preclinical models, GLP-1 receptor activation has been associated with engagement of intracellular signaling pathways, including PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β, cAMP/PKA/CREB, and AMPK/SIRT1, and several studies report reduced neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and amyloid-β or α-synuclein accumulation. These findings are not uniform: recent studies in preventive and established Alzheimer's disease mouse models found no benefit of semaglutide or tirzepatide, and the phase 3 EVOKE/EVOKE+ trials of oral semaglutide in early Alzheimer's disease did not slow clinical progression. GLP-1 RAs are also frequently associated with shifts in gut microbiota composition, including enrichment of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, which supports a biologically plausible gut-brain axis interaction. However, microbiota responses are heterogeneous and context-dependent, and no included study used causal designs such as germ-free models or fecal microbiota transplantation. Whether neuroprotective effects arise from direct central receptor engagement, from peripheral metabolic effects, or from microbiota remodeling therefore remains unresolved, and microbiota changes may be a secondary consequence of metabolic improvement rather than a mediator of therapeutic effect.

papers.title: The Growing Role of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Neuropsychiatry.
papers.abstract: The co-occurrence of metabolic and psychiatric disorders poses a major challenge in medicine, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have emerged as candidates for neuropsychiatric repurposing given the wide distribution of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors in brain regions governing mood, cognition, and reward. This narrative review summarizes central and peripheral mechanisms linking GLP-1 signaling to neuropsychiatric outcomes, critically appraises clinical evidence across psychiatric and neurodegenerative domains, and proposes a framework for integrating GLP-1RAs into neuropsychiatric care. A targeted search of PubMed/MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov (January 2015-August 2026) prioritized randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and prospective cohorts reporting neuropsychiatric outcomes. Four converging mechanisms- neuroinflammation, metabolic-vascular neuroprotection, synaptic plasticity, and mesolimbic reward modulation- underpin this rationale. The strongest and most clinically actionable evidence supports GLP-1RA use for antipsychotic-induced metabolic dysfunction, with trials in clozapine/olanzapine-treated patients showing substantial weight loss and glycemic normalization without psychiatric worsening or altered clozapine levels. By contrast, in Alzheimer's disease, despite consistent observational signals of 33-53% dementia risk reduction, Phase 3 EVOKE/EVOKE+ trials found no benefit of oral semaglutide in early symptomatic disease despite biomarker engagement, favoring a prevention- rather than treatment-focused framework. Evidence in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder remains more limited: motor benefit in Parkinson's disease appears restricted to short-acting agents, with the largest phase 3 trial negative, while broad antidepressant efficacy is unsupported, although semaglutide improved effort-based decision-making in anhedonic, metabolically burdened patients. papers.title: Butyrate and the brain-gut axis in Parkinson's disease: From microbial metabolite to potential therapeutic target.
papers.journal: The Journal of international medical research
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with substantial unmet therapeutic needs. This narrative review synthesizes current mechanistic and clinical evidence on the role of the gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid butyrate in the brain-gut axis in Parkinson's disease. Mechanistically, experimental studies suggest that butyrate reinforces intestinal barrier integrity and modulates intestinal immune responses, with enteric glial and vagal pathways providing possible links to central neuroinflammation. Its effects on microglial inflammatory phenotypes and autophagic clearance of α-synuclein, including possible cholinergic mediation, require further validation. We critically evaluated the strengths and limitations of this evidence, discussed inconsistent findings across cohorts, and summarized clinical studies on butyrate-related interventions, including butyrate supplementation, dietary fiber, probiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation. Although preclinical evidence is substantial and context dependent, clinical translation is constrained by small and heterogeneous human cohorts, unresolved butyrate bioavailability, optimal dose and route of administration, long-term safety concerns, variability of the gut microbiota, and the absence of randomized evidence establishing butyrate-specific disease modification. Microglial heterogeneity revealed by single-cell transcriptomic studies also challenges the classical M1/M2 framework. We conclude by proposing priorities for future research, including well-powered randomized trials, standardized butyrate and microbiome measurements, patient stratification, and single-cell investigations.

papers.title: Degeneration of Nigrostriatal Dopaminergic Axons in Parkinson's Disease: Mechanisms and Potential Diagnostic and Treatment Strategies.
papers.abstract: According to conventional wisdom, progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is the central pathological event in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, recent evidence suggests that nigrostriatal dopaminergic axons and presynaptic terminals may be affected in the early stages of the disease. This article integrates evidence from human autopsies, molecular imaging, and experimental models regarding the early involvement of dopaminergic axons and presynaptic terminals. The discussion focuses on potential mechanisms such as α-synuclein (α-syn)-mediated presynaptic dysfunction, axonal transport impairment, mitochondrial homeostasis imbalance, and SARM1-NAD+

papers.title: Midbrain Slice Culture as an Ex Vivo Analysis Platform for Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder of the motor system. It is characterized by the accumulation of intracellular α-synuclein aggregates forming Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. Consequently, PD is recognized as the most common synucleinopathy. The motor symptoms of the disease result from the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain, leading to a significant dopamine deficit. Although PD has been studied extensively using traditional in vitro and in vivo models, discrepancies in their findings highlight the necessity of experimental platforms that more closely mimic the brain's complex environment. To effectively analyze this progressive disorder, a system is required that preserves neural circuitry and is amenable to long-term observation and manipulation. This chapter provides a practical, step-by-step method to prepare and cultivate organotypic midbrain tissue slices as a powerful ex vivo experimental model.

papers.title: Early DNA repair and stress response signatures in prodromal Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson’s disease begins years before motor symptoms appear. Longitudinal blood transcriptomics shows that DNA repair and stress response pathways are most altered during this prodromal phase, then lose discriminative power in established disease. In this Comment, we link these changes to aging-related DNA damage and consider their biomarker potential. Mirroring aging hallmarks, they suggest a prodromal intervention window, when mechanisms driving dopaminergic neuron vulnerability are most active and potentially tractable.

papers.title: Common Marmoset Model of Alpha-Synuclein Propagation.
papers.abstract: Understanding the propagation of alpha-synuclein (αS) aggregates is critical for elucidating the pathological mechanisms of synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy. Here, we describe a protocol for generating a nonhuman primate model of αS propagation by intracerebral injection of synthetic αS preformed fibrils (PFFs) into the common marmose (Callithrix jacchus).  This protocol allows phosphorylated αS pathology and its propagation to be detected at 3 months post-injection, providing a valuable nonhuman primate model for studying synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Electron-Microscopic Analysis of α-Synuclein Fibrils.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein (α-syn) is a major component of abnormal protein deposits observed in the brains of patients with synucleinopathies, including Lewy body disease and multiple system atrophy. The synaptic protein α-syn is water-soluble under normal physiological conditions, but in these patients' brains, we see accumulation of insoluble amyloid-like α-syn fibrils with prion-like properties. Intracerebral accumulation of these fibrils is correlated with disease onset and progression. Recombinant α-syn protein also forms amyloid-like fibrils that are structurally akin to those extracted from patients' brains. Recent cryo-electron microscopy studies have revealed the core structures of α-syn fibrils formed in vitro under various conditions and those extracted from synucleinopathy brains at the atomic level. In this chapter, we describe negative staining and immuno-electron microscopy protocols for ultrastructural characterization of synthetic α-syn fibrils and patient-derived α-syn fibrils.

papers.title: Amphiphilic red fluorescent emissive carbon dots crossing the blood-brain barrier for imaging phase separation of α-synuclein.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by pathological α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation arising from dysregulated phase separation, yielding α-syn condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and α-syn fibrils (α-syn-F) via liquid-solid phase separation (LSPS). It is meaningful to visualize the phase separation of α-syn for in-depth understanding of PD pathology. Herein, an amphiphilic Congo red-derived carbon dot, named as RP-2, was rationally designed. The RP-2 showed turn-on red fluorescence towards α-syn-F rather than monomer, and was utilized as the probe to detect α-syn-F in complex matrices. Besides, the RP-2 could label α-syn condensates without affecting the dynamic characteristics of LLPS, and stain α-syn-F in living cells. Using RP-2 as the staining dye, α-syn condensates were demonstrated to recruit β-synuclein, illustrating that β-synuclein could regulate the α-syn aggregation. Particularly, due to introduction of D-phenylalanine as the carbon source, the RP-2 exhibited enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration with the aid of large neutral amino acid transporter 1. Thus, the RP-2 successfully imaged cerebral α-syn-F of A53T mice, and distinguished them from normal ones. The present study offered a feasible method to construct amphiphilic CDs with BBB penetration for visualizing the phase separation of α-syn.

papers.title: Preparation of Oligodendrocyte Culture on Decellularized Brain Tissue.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by pathological accumulation of α-synuclein protein but fundamentally differ in the cellular location of α-synuclein aggregates. In PD, α-synuclein forms intraneuronal Lewy bodies, whereas MSA is uniquely defined by α-synuclein inclusions within oligodendrocytes, termed glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs). Understanding oligodendroglial dysfunction in these synucleinopathies therefore requires experimental models that recapitulate the physiologically relevant cellular microenvironments. Traditional two-dimensional culture systems are unable to reproduce key features of the brain's native extracellular matrix (ECM), which plays essential roles in regulating oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) migration, differentiation, and myelination. Here, we describe detailed protocols for culturing oligosphere-derived cells on decellularized mouse brain tissue that preserves the native ECM architecture, composition, and mechanical properties. When combined with an optimized oligodendrocyte differentiation buffer, this system promotes enhanced differentiation of oligodendrocyte lineage cells, particularly GPR17-expressing intermediate-stage oligodendrocytes, which are difficult to maintain in conventional cultures. This platform provides a physiologically relevant model for investigating oligodendroglial dysfunction, α-synuclein accumulation, and therapeutic strategies targeting remyelination in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: α-Synuclein Seeding Assay Using RT-QuIC.
papers.abstract: α-Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the misfolding and aggregation of α-synuclein (α-Syn). These conditions are thought to involve distinct conformational strains of αSyn aggregates that drive self-propagation and cell-to-cell transmission, with aggregation occurring via a seeded polymerization mechanism. The real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assay, originally developed for prion proteins, has been adapted to detect αSyn seeds. More recently, it has been broadly referred to as the seed amplification assay (SAA), a general term describing methods that amplify and detect minute amounts of misfolded protein aggregates. By incorporating the fluorescent dye thioflavin-T, this method enables real-time monitoring of aggregation kinetics with high sensitivity, allowing the detection of seed aggregates at extremely low levels. When used for diagnostic purposes, αSyn RT-QuIC shows high specificity (82%-100%) and variable sensitivity (70%-100%) across studies. It also provides insights into the biochemical properties of distinct αSyn strains. Recent advances have expanded αSyn SAA (RT-QuIC) to blood-based specimens, particularly via immunoprecipitation-coupled RT-QuIC, enabling minimally invasive diagnosis. Quantitative measures, such as the Lewy-fold pathology score and kinetic parameters, further allow assessment of disease progression and therapeutic response. In addition, skin biopsy SAA (RT-QuIC) offers a peripheral diagnostic alternative with accuracy comparable to that of cerebrospinal fluid-based methods. Here, we describe detailed protocols for αSyn SAA (RT-QuIC) assays.

papers.title: α-Synuclein Propagation Mouse Models of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is pathologically characterized by intraneuronal α-Synuclein (α-Syn) inclusions called Lewy bodies (LBs) and by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc). Autopsy studies have suggested that Lewy pathology initially occurs in the olfactory bulb and enteric nervous system and subsequently spreads throughout the brain in a stereotypical manner. Recent studies have demonstrated that templated fibrillization and intercellular dissemination of misfolded α-Syn underlie this pathological progression. Injection of animals with α-Syn preformed fibrils (PFFs) can recapitulate LB-like inclusions and subsequent intercellular transmission of α-Syn pathology. Moreover, targeting specific brain regions or peripheral tissues enables the generation of distinct models depending on the injection site. These features of α-Syn PFF-injected animal models provide a platform for exploring disease mechanisms and testing disease-modifying therapies in PD research. Here, we describe methods for the generation of α-Syn PFFs and their administration in mice.

papers.title: Feasibility and acceptability of high-intensity interval training for apathy after deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease: the HIIT-ing apathy study protocol.
The somato-cognitive action network in parkinsonian gait dysfunction and closed-loop neuromodulation.
papers.abstract: Parkinsonian gait dysfunction and freezing of gait (FoG) emerge from interactions among motor, cognitive-control and neuromodulatory systems. The somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) adds an anatomically defined cortical component to these distributed accounts. This narrative review examines its contribution across disease associations, targeted perturbation, state-contingent treatment, and incremental clinical value. SCAN-subcortical hyperconnectivity in Parkinson's disease and its treatment sensitivity link inter-effector cortex to established disease circuits. A randomized comparison of individualized SCAN and effector-region intermittent theta-burst stimulation supports target-dependent improvement in total motor scores; FoG-specific efficacy remains unresolved because the axial outcome combined gait and non-gait items. In parallel, gait-phase and activity-dependent deep-brain stimulation demonstrate that neural signals can guide behaviorally timed treatment, with early benefits in selected gait outcomes. Across these accounts, neurochemical and distributed-network measures characterize vulnerability, while episode-linked decoupling identifies candidate state markers. SCAN contributes a more specific cortical hypothesis: transition-related activity in individually mapped SCAN may distinguish impending freezing beyond neighboring cortex and established gait signals. Cortical target selection and adaptive timing have separate empirical support; their combination is a proposed therapeutic strategy. Matched input and stimulation comparisons can determine whether SCAN adds predictive information or clinical benefit to existing controllers.

papers.title: An Italian auditory gender Stroop walking task: feasibility and preliminary cognitive-motor performance profiling in neurological populations.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Stroop-based paradigms are widely used to probe inhibitory control during locomotion, although auditory Stroop walking tasks remain underexplored in neurological populations. This study introduced an Italian auditory adaptation of the Gender Stroop task and provided a preliminary methodological evaluation of its feasibility and of multidimensional gait, accuracy and verbal-timing information obtained during walking. METHODS: Forty participants were included: 24 individuals with neurological conditions (multiple sclerosis, n RESULTS: Hierarchical clustering of 15 standardized gait variables identified a higher-performance profile (n DISCUSSION: Overall, the Italian auditory Gender Stroop walking task was feasible and allowed concurrent assessment of gait and cognitive-verbal performance during a structured cognitive-motor task. Larger, age-balanced and independent samples are required to establish the reproducibility of the gait-performance structure and determine the additional contribution of Stroop accuracy and verbal-timing measures beyond general locomotor performance.

papers.title: Deep Brain Stimulation Using Animal Models of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: The use of deep brain stimulation (DBS) as a therapy for neurological disorders, especially Parkinson's disease (PD), is widely applied in the field of functional neurosurgery. Both the subthalamic nucleus and the globus pallidus interna are major targets for PD. Experimental DBS is performed using animal models to evaluate new indications and promote advancements in technology. In this article, we reviewed our experience with the concept of experimental DBS, including its development and validation. The following work aims to establish that experimental DBS in animals is an adequate tool for exploring new indications for DBS and to further refine DBS technology.

papers.title: A proposed cholinergic phenotype of Parkinson's disease: candidate clinical, biofluid, and imaging markers.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Various non-motor symptom (NMS)-dominant clinical subtypes are recognised in Parkinson's disease (PD), and a cognitive dysfunction-dominant "cholinergic subtype" has also been proposed. Cognitive impairment of varying degrees occurs in the prodromal phase of PD and is partly related to dysfunction of central cholinergic pathways, which can contribute to varying clinical phenotypes. In a subset of patients with PD, a cognitive dysfunction-dominant phenotype identified using clinical tests can be recognised and has been termed the "cholinergic" subtype. In this narrative review of the proposed cholinergic subtype, we provide details of clinical, biofluid, and imaging markers that may help further define and refine this non-motor subtype of PD, although the majority of biomarkers remain exploratory. METHODS: We reviewed the available English-language literature published between 2000 and 2025 that was identified through Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science. RESULTS: Based on the cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Cambridgeshire Parkinson's Incidence from GP to Neurologist (CamPaIGN) study, we identified two clinical tests-copying an intersecting pentagon and assessing semantic fluency-as the clinical anchors and constructed a clinical phenotype of late-onset PD characterised by hyposmia, constipation, low body weight, high frailty, gait dysfunction, and other cognitive and neuropsychiatric deficits as associated features. Potential biomarkers, such as plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and imaging of the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), remain exploratory and need to be studied in well-enriched and well-characterised cholinergic PD cohorts. CONCLUSION: This narrative review describes a proposed clinical phenotype of the cholinergic subtype of PD, which needs to be validated, and highlights that the majority of biomarkers remain exploratory.

papers.title: Drug Delivery to the Brain of Parkinson's Disease Mouse Using an Osmotic Pump and Methods for Evaluating Motor Performance.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by progressive resting tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, gait disturbances, postural instability, and dementia. The symptoms of PD are closely linked to the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The loss of these neurons in some mouse models of PD results in abnormal motor performance, including abnormal limb-clasping reflexes, abnormal footprint patterns, and lower rotarod performance than littermate wild-type mice. When evaluating the efficacy of potential therapeutic molecules in mice, their administration to mice requires consideration of the blood-brain barrier. Therefore, the long-term administration of agents directly into the mouse brain using an osmotic pump to bypass the blood-brain barrier is a crucial method for assessing drug efficacy in these models. Here, we describe methods for the direct administration of low-molecular-weight compounds into the mouse brain using an osmotic pump, and also for the evaluation of motor performance, namely, footprint analysis and the limb-clasping test. These techniques may also be applicable to other neurodegenerative diseases in addition to PD.

papers.title: [Research progress on the mechanism of acupuncture in protecting the intestinal barrier to intervene in Parkinson's disease].
papers.journal: Zhen ci yan jiu = Acupuncture research
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence from recent years indicates a strong association between PD pathogenesis and gut-brain axis dysfunction, with impairment of the intestinal barrier being recognized as a critical initiating factor. This review summarizes current research on the multi-target mechanisms through which acupuncture protects the intestinal barrier and thereby intervenes in PD progression. Evidence suggests that acupuncture can restore gut microbiota homeostasis by increasing short-chain fatty acids and reducing lipopolysaccharide levels; upregulate the expression of tight junction proteins (zonula occludens-1, occludin) and mucin (Muc 2), thereby directly reinforcing the intestinal physical barrier; effectively clear aberrant α-Syn aggregates in the colon and suppress the NOD-like receptor 3 and nuclear factor κB pathway to alleviate intestinal inflammation. These mechanisms act synergistically to maintain intestinal barrier integrity and block the transmission of pathological signals from the gut to the brain.

papers.title: Resting-state EEG features of cognitive fluctuations across the Lewy body disease spectrum.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive fluctuations (CF) are a core feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) that negatively impact quality of life. Despite their prevalence and negative impact, CF are challenging to identify clinically. The goal of this study was to identify easily obtainable EEG features associated with CF across the spectrum of Lewy body disease (LB). METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 53 patients prospectively enrolled through the outpatient clinics of the Department of Neurology at Virginia Commonwealth University. Based on the Clinician Assessment of Fluctuations, participants were categorized as LB disease without CF (LB-CF) or LB disease with CF (LB + CF). All participants underwent a resting-state EEG recording with eyes closed for at least 3 min. EEG data were preprocessed and the following features were extracted: dominant frequency (DF), dominant frequency variability (DFV), dominant frequency prevalence (DFP), and individual alpha peak frequency (IAF). We applied Kruskal-Wallis tests and logistic regression models to evaluate differences in EEG features between study groups. RESULTS: We analyzed EEG features for 29 LB + CF and 24 LB-CF participants. Compared to the LB-CF group, the LB + CF group had significantly lower DF, DFP-alpha, and IAF in all derivations (all p < 0.05). In logistic regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, and MoCA score, these EEG features remained significant predictors of group (LB + CF vs. LB-CF, all q < 0.05). The elastic-net logistic regression model identified five predictors (anterior DFP-alpha, anterior DFP-pre-alpha, anterior DF, temporal DF, and temporal IAF) achieving an AUC of 0.86, whereas anterior DFP-alpha alone achieved an AUC of 0.85. CONCLUSION: Among patients with LB disease, resting-state EEG features were associated with CF and were significant predictors of CF even after adjustment for age, sex, and MoCA. The

papers.title: The Functional Assessment of LRRK2 in Caenorhabditis elegans Mechanosensory Neurons.
papers.abstract: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) is a powerful model organism to systematically analyze the functions of genes of interest in vivo. Especially, C. elegans nervous system is suitable for morphological and functional analyses of neuronal genes due to its optical transparency of the body and well-established anatomy, including neural connections. The C. elegans ortholog of Parkinson's disease-associated gene LRRK2, named lrk-1, has been shown to play a role in the regulation of axonal morphology in a subset of neurons. Here I describe the detailed methodologies for the assessment of LRK-1/LRRK2 function as well as the analysis of genetic interaction involving lrk-1/LRRK2 by performing live imaging of C. elegans mechanosensory neurons.

papers.title: GBA1 Parkinson's disease: peculiarities in Asia and India.
GBA1 Parkinson's disease: peculiarities in Asia and India.
Fluorescence-Based Assay to Monitor GCase Activity in Cultured Cells.
papers.abstract: Glucosylceramide (GlcCer), a member of glycolipids, is degraded by β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase, GBA). Although GlcCer is synthesized by a sole GlcCer synthase, four GCases have been identified in mammals to date. Heterozygous mutations in the lysosomal GBA (GBA1) gene are the most potent risk factor for developing Parkinson's disease (PD). Although it is not clear why GBA1 heterozygous mutations are involved in the pathogenesis of PD, GBA1 heterozygous mutations reduce not only GBA1 activity but also nonlysosomal GCase (GBA2) activity. Therefore, abnormal lipid metabolism due to loss of both enzymes is likely to be involved in disease development. In this chapter, I describe a protocol to measure GBA1 and GBA2 activity in cultured cells using a fluorescent GlcCer analogue.

papers.title: Detection of Substrate Phosphorylation of Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase 2 in Tissues and Cultured Cells.
papers.abstract: Recent studies revealed that leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) phosphorylates several Rab proteins under physiological conditions. Mutations linked with familial Parkinso'n disease cause an abnormal increase in the Rab phosphorylation, which has not been elucidated in an in vitro kinase assay where artificial peptide substrates are often used. Here, we provide protocols for detecting the LRRK2 activity in tissues and cultured cells using Rab phosphorylation as a readout.

papers.title: Methods to Analyze LRRK2 Functions Under Lysosomal Stress: Evaluation of Lysosomal Secretion and Morphological Alteration.
papers.abstract: Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is a causative gene product of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease and has been shown to play a role in lysosomal regulation. We have previously shown that, under lysosomal stress conditions such as chloroquine treatment, endogenous LRRK2 recruits its substrates Rab8a and Rab10 onto overloaded lysosomes through their phosphorylation and functions in the suppression of lysosomal enlargement as well as the promotion of the exocytic release of lysosomal hydrolases. In this chapter, we introduce methods to analyze cellular functions of LRRK2 in RAW264.7 cells exposed to lysosomal stress as an update to the protocol described in the previous edition.
